strengths: Compelling and timely motivation: Bridges modern linear state space / linear recurrent operator formulations (e.g., LRU, parallel associative scan) with Reservoir Computing (RC), effectively eliminating the sequential bottleneck and quadratic parameter scaling of traditional dense reservoirs.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation: Evaluates across diverse domains including memory capacity benchmarks, chaotic dynamical systems (Lorenz, Mackey-Glass), real-world forecasting (ETT), multivariate UCR classification, and long-sequence pixel-level classification (sMNIST, psMNIST).

Strong computational and efficiency gains: Consistently demonstrates significant wall-clock speedups, lower energy usage, and reduced carbon footprints compared to sequential ESNs and fully trainable sequence models (LSTM, Transformer, LRU, Mamba), while retaining or exceeding predictive accuracy.

Well-structured presentation and extensive reproducibility details: The paper is clearly written, includes complete complexity analyses (Table 5), detailed hyperparameter exploration grids, and hyperparameter sensitivity ablations in the appendix.
weaknesses: Incremental theoretical contributions: Theorem 4.1 (ESP condition on eigenvalues) is an immediate consequence of decoupled diagonal linear dynamics. Proposition 4.2 relies on standard matrix diagonalization ($W_h = V \Lambda_h V^{-1}$), which assumes diagonalizability (ignoring defective matrices) and shifts the dense coupling into the projection $V$, whereas the actual empirical model uses a constrained 1-D convolutional mixing layer rather than a full matrix projection.

Blurring of the RC paradigm on complex benchmarks: On sMNIST and psMNIST, the readout is parametrized as a Multi-Layer Perceptron trained with backpropagation via Adam over up to 100 epochs, departing from the classic closed-form / single-pass linear regression paradigm of Reservoir Computing.

Scope of parallel scan benefits: While the associative scan reduces parallel depth to logarithmic time on parallel hardware (GPUs), online streaming inference or edge microcontroller deployment—traditional niches for RC—remains inherently sequential, where parallel prefix scans offer limited advantage.

strengths: The paper addresses a fundamental bottleneck in Reservoir Computing (RC)—sequential time processing and quadratic parameter/memory scaling—by introducing a principled, complex-diagonal linear recurrence that can be parallelized via associative scan.

The theoretical framing is sound and clear: the authors derive exact necessary and sufficient conditions for the Echo State Property (Theorem 4.1) in the complex diagonal case and connect the model to universality guarantees for linear reservoirs with fading memory.

The proposed architectural design is well thought out: using complex diagonal transitions reduces memory from O(N_h^2) to O(N_h), allowing reservoirs to scale to over 100,000 neurons where traditional ESNs run out of memory, while the 1D convolutional mixer provides non-linear cross-channel interaction with minimal parameter overhead.

The experimental evaluation is thorough and convincing, spanning synthetic memory tasks, chaotic system forecasting, real-world multivariate time series (ETT), UCR/UEA classification benchmarks, and long-range pixel classification (sMNIST/psMNIST), accompanied by runtime, energy, and carbon emission profiling.
weaknesses: The conceptual leap from existing linear state-space models and recurrent units (specifically LRU by Orvieto et al., 2023) is somewhat evolutionary: it largely consists of freezing the LRU recurrent parameters and placing an RC readout (or mixer) on top.

There is a gap between the theoretical equivalence claim (Proposition 4.2) and the actual implementation: the proof relies on an arbitrary MLP readout applied to the linear state, whereas the practical model fixes an untrained 1-D convolutional mixing layer with tanh activation before a linear or shallow MLP readout.

For the sMNIST and psMNIST tasks, the readout is implemented and trained as a 2-layer MLP using backpropagation and Adam (Section F.2) rather than a convex/closed-form linear solver (e.g., ridge regression via SVD). This weakens the standard RC premise of completely avoiding gradient-based optimization.

strengths: Clear motivation and timely bridge between Reservoir Computing (RC) and modern State Space Models (SSMs): The paper identifies two fundamental bottlenecks in RC—strictly sequential recurrent execution and the quadratic memory footprint of dense reservoir matrices—and addresses them by adopting complex diagonal linear recurrence parallelizable via associative scan.

Substantial computational and memory efficiency gains: The empirical results demonstrate that ParalESN scales logarithmically with sequence length via parallel associative scan (Figure 2, left) and can scale to high-dimensional reservoirs (e.g., over 100K reservoir units) where conventional dense ESNs run out of memory (Figure 2, right). Training times across synthetic, chaotic, and real-world benchmarks show up to order-of-magnitude speedups compared to standard and deep ESNs.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation: The authors validate the method across memory-based benchmarks (MemCap, ctXOR, SinMem), forecasting tasks (Lorenz96, Mackey-Glass, NARMA, ETT datasets), UCR/UEA classification tasks, and pixel-level classification (sMNIST, psMNIST). Comparisons include both RC baselines (ESN, deep ESN, SCR, Structured RC) and fully trained sequence models (LSTM, Transformer, LRU, Mamba), including energy and CO2 tracking via CodeCarbon.

Theoretical characterization of stability: Theorem 4.1 provides exact necessary and sufficient conditions for the Echo State Property (ESP) on the complex diagonal transition matrix, directly relating stability to the moduli of the sampled diagonal entries.
weaknesses: Incremental architectural novelty: The core mechanism—diagonal recurrence in the complex domain parameterized by magnitude and phase, solved via parallel associative scan—is directly adopted from the Linear Recurrent Unit (LRU; Orvieto et al., 2023) and diagonal SSMs (S5). The primary adaptation is fixing these recurrent weights without training and adding an untrained 1-D convolution mixer.

Limited depth in theoretical contributions: Proposition 4.2 and its corollary are straightforward consequences of the standard Jordan/eigendecomposition ($W_h = V \Lambda V^{-1}$) applied to linear dynamical systems and existing universality results for linear reservoirs (Grigoryeva & Ortega, 2018a;b). They do not account for the specific 1-D convolutional mixing layer or deep multi-layer stacking used in practice.

Inconsistent readout / optimization setup across benchmarks: For standard time series and UCR benchmarks, the readout is trained via closed-form ridge regression (SVD), whereas for sMNIST and psMNIST, the readout is an MLP trained with Adam over 100 epochs using backpropagation (Section F.2). Introducing a multi-layer gradient-trained head deviates from the classical RC paradigm and confounds whether performance gains stem from the reservoir or the trained non-linear head.

Evaluation on long-context sequence benchmarks is limited: Given that the primary motivation is enabling efficient, parallel scaling on long sequences (drawing direct inspiration from LRU and Mamba), the paper restricts its empirical evaluation to relatively short or standard RC datasets (e.g., sequences of length 500 to 5,000) and MNIST variants, omitting challenging long-sequence benchmarks like the Long Range Arena (LRA) where modern SSMs typically demonstrate their edge.
